pos: n. phr. (those fitted to destruction, on whom God shews His wrath)
etymology: Greek skeuē orgēs — skeuos, a vessel, implement, or article made for a use; and orgē, settled wrath or indignation. The figure is the potter's, carried on from Romans 9:21.
biblical_def: Paul answers the objector who charges God with injustice in election by appealing first to the potter: “Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?” He then puts the matter as a question: “What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction.” Two features of the verse govern its doctrine and are regularly missed. The first is longsuffering. The vessels of wrath are not described as swept away but as endured, and endured with much longsuffering — the sentence is about restraint, not haste. The second is the voice of the verbs, and the asymmetry is deliberate. Here the vessels are “fitted to destruction”, a participle with no stated agent; in the next verse the vessels of mercy are those whom “he had afore prepared unto glory”, where God is named as the one preparing. Scripture does not balance election and reprobation as two identical acts. God prepares the one; the other is fitted, and Romans has already spent three chapters showing how men fit themselves, being without excuse. The chapter's purpose is not speculative. Paul is defending God's freedom against the charge of unrighteousness, and the answer he gives is that the Creator owes no man the grace He gives to another.

corruption_summary: The passage is softened into a statement about national roles or escaped altogether, and where it is held it is often pressed into a symmetry Paul's own grammar refuses.
corruption_paragraphs: The most common evasion reduces Romans 9 to a discussion of corporate roles in redemptive history — Israel and the nations, service and vocation — with no bearing on the eternal state of individuals. The chapter will not sustain it. Paul begins in grief over his kinsmen's personal unbelief, instances Jacob and Esau as individuals before either had done good or evil, and raises the objection every honest reader raises: why doth he yet find fault? That objection only arises if individual destiny is in view. The arminian resolution, which makes election a response to foreseen faith, relocates the decisive act from God to man and leaves Paul's objector with no objection to make.

The opposite error over-corrects into a flat symmetry, in which God is said to create men for hell precisely as He creates men for glory, by the same kind of act. The verse's own grammar refuses that equal ultimacy. The vessels of mercy are those whom God afore prepared; the vessels of wrath are fitted to destruction, with no agent named, after eight chapters establishing that men are without excuse and have earned their condemnation. The Reformed tradition has guarded this asymmetry carefully, and a preacher who loses it will preach a God who damns the innocent, which Scripture never does. The principle to recover is the tone as much as the content: Paul holds this doctrine with great heaviness and continual sorrow in his heart, and anyone who holds it with relish has not learnt it from him.

pos: n. phr. (those whom God afore prepared unto glory)
etymology: Greek skeuē eleous — skeuos, a vessel or implement, and eleos, mercy or pity. The potter figure of Romans 9:21 governs the phrase.
biblical_def: The counterpart of the vessels of wrath is named in the next verse: “And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory, Even us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles?” Every clause carries doctrine. The vessels are of mercy, which is the word for pity shown to the wretched, so that nothing in them is the ground of their selection; mercy by definition is not owed. God afore prepared them, and here, unlike the preceding verse, the agent is named and the act is God's — this is the asymmetry the Reformed tradition has always marked between election and reprobation. The preparation is unto glory, which names the end of the whole work, the glorification that closes the chain of Romans 8. And Paul then does something the system-builders often forget: he identifies the vessels. “Even us, whom he hath called” — the doctrine lands on the reader, and the called include Gentiles, which was the scandal the chapter was written to defend. The stated purpose of the arrangement is that God “might make known the riches of his glory”. Election is not an administrative sorting; it exists so that the riches of glory should be displayed on people who had no claim to them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Mercy, that benevolence or tenderness which disposes to forgive and to relieve. Vessels of mercy, Romans 9:23, those whom God afore prepared unto glory, that He might make known the riches of His glory.
webster_full: Mercy, tenderness which inclines to forgive injuries and relieve the wretched.
Greek eleos, mercy, pity shown toward the miserable.

corruption_summary: Election is recast as God's response to foreseen faith, which makes mercy a wage; or it is held coldly, as a status to be claimed rather than the riches of glory displayed on the undeserving.
corruption_paragraphs: The arminian construction makes election conditional upon foreseen faith, so that God chooses those He knows will choose Him. However devoutly intended, this empties the word mercy. What is given in view of something foreseen in the recipient is not mercy but recognition, and the decisive movement has been relocated from God to the man. Paul's whole argument runs the other way: the preparing is afore, the vessels are of mercy, and the parallel in Ephesians grounds it in God being rich in mercy toward those who were dead in sins. A dead man contributes nothing to be foreseen.

The error among those who hold the doctrine is one of temperature. Election can be treated as a membership status, a mark of belonging to the discerning party, and the tell is a tone of cool superiority toward those outside. Romans 9:23 forecloses it by naming the purpose: that God might make known the riches of his glory. The doctrine exists to display His glory on people who had no claim, which leaves the vessel nothing to be proud of — the clay has no part in its own choosing. Paul's own posture in the same passage is great heaviness over the unbelieving, and his conclusion two chapters later is doxology rather than a chart. The principle to recover is that the doctrine of election should produce wonder and tenderness, and that where it produces complacency it has been misunderstood at the root.

pos: n. phr. (the condition from which Paul cries to be delivered, Romans 7:24)
etymology: Greek to sōma tou thanatou toutou — sōma, body, and thanatos, death. The phrase may be read as the body belonging to this death, or as this body of death.
biblical_def: At the end of his account of the inward war Paul breaks into a cry: “O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” The answer follows at once: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin.” The phrase gathers the whole chapter. It is not a complaint about the physical body as such, which Paul elsewhere calls the temple of the Holy Ghost and expects to be redeemed; it names the whole condition of a man in whom indwelling sin still operates — what he has just described as evil present with him when he would do good. The cry is who, not what: Paul does not ask for a technique but for a deliverer, and the answer is a Person. Reformed exposition has generally taken the speaker to be the regenerate man, and the grammar supports it, for an unconverted man does not delight in the law of God after the inward man. That reading is the pastorally decisive one, because it means this wretchedness is the normal experience of a true Christian and not evidence against his conversion. Thanksgiving and unfinished conflict stand in the same breath. The deliverance is certain and already given in Christ, and the warfare continues until the body itself is redeemed.

corruption_summary: The cry is treated as a stage the mature Christian leaves behind, or else as evidence that Paul was not yet converted, and either way the believer's ordinary experience of indwelling sin is made abnormal.
corruption_paragraphs: Perfectionist and higher-life teaching has long read Romans 7 as the condition of a defeated Christian who has not yet entered the victorious life of Romans 8, so that a believer who recognises himself in verse 24 is told he is living below his privileges. The pastoral damage is considerable: sincere Christians conclude that their continuing struggle is a failure of consecration, and they oscillate between pretended victory and private despair. Paul gives no such ladder. Thanksgiving for deliverance and the acknowledgment of serving the law of sin with the flesh stand in the same verse, and Romans 8 itself still groans, waiting for the redemption of the body.

The opposite reading makes the speaker an unregenerate man under conviction, which removes the difficulty by removing Paul. It founders on verse 22, where the speaker delights in the law of God after the inward man — a thing Romans 8:7 says the carnal mind cannot do. The therapeutic culture then adds a third distortion by renaming the whole experience as shame to be resolved rather than sin to be fought, so that the cry becomes a symptom and the deliverer becomes unnecessary. Scripture's own shape should be kept exactly: a real wretchedness, honestly named; a real deliverance, already secured in Christ; and a real conflict that continues until the body is redeemed. The principle to recover is that assurance and struggle are not rivals in the Christian life.

pos: n. phr. (of Gentiles who, lacking the written law, shew its work in their hearts)
etymology: Greek heautois eisin nomos, they are a law to themselves, from nomos, law, and the reflexive heautois. The Authorized Version renders it a law unto themselves.
biblical_def: Paul writes, “For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves: Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another.” The meaning is the opposite of what the modern idiom suggests. Paul is not describing men who make their own rules; he is describing men who, without ever receiving Sinai, nevertheless display the law's work written in their hearts. They are a law to themselves in the sense that the standard is present within them rather than delivered to them on tablets — the same law, differently supplied. The evidence Paul cites is the operation of conscience: it bears witness, and the thoughts accuse or else excuse. He is not crediting the Gentiles with righteousness. The argument of the whole section is that this inward law leaves them without excuse, exactly as the written law leaves the Jew without excuse, so that every mouth may be stopped and all the world become guilty before God. The passage is therefore the New Testament's clearest statement that moral knowledge is universal, that no man is genuinely ignorant of the standard he breaks, and that conscience, though not infallible, is a real witness God has placed in every man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Law, a rule of action prescribed by authority. A law unto themselves, Romans 2:14, of Gentiles who, not having the written law, shew the work of the law written in their hearts.
webster_full: Law, a rule of action prescribed by a supreme authority.
Greek nomos, law; heautois, to themselves, the reflexive pronoun.

corruption_summary: The idiom has been exactly inverted: in common English “a law unto himself” now means a man who answers to no standard, which is the reverse of what Paul says.
corruption_paragraphs: The ordinary modern use of the phrase describes someone who disregards rules and does as he pleases — a maverick, an operator, a man accountable to nobody. That is the precise opposite of Romans 2:14, where being a law unto themselves means the law is present in them, written on the heart, so that they are accountable without having been handed a copy. The reversal is not merely a curiosity of usage; it has made the verse unreadable to English speakers and removed from circulation the one text that most directly asserts that moral obligation is universal and inescapable.

The inversion matches the age's actual doctrine, which is autonomy — from autos and nomos, self-law — the belief that each person authors the standard by which he is to be judged. Paul's claim is the flat denial of this. The law is written on the heart by Another, and the proof is the stubborn behaviour of conscience, which goes on accusing and excusing whether or not a man grants it jurisdiction. This should be stated with the care Paul uses: conscience is a witness, not a lawgiver, and a conscience may be seared or poorly informed and must itself be instructed by Scripture. The principle to recover is that no one is morally ignorant, that the Gentile without the Bible and the church member with one are both without excuse, and that the universal witness of conscience is part of why the gospel can be preached to every man.

pos: n. phr. (the civil authorities, as ordained of God)
etymology: Greek hai ousai exousiai, the existing authorities, from exousia, authority or right, and the participle of eimi, to be. The Authorized Version's that be is the older English for that exist.
biblical_def: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.” The English that be means simply that exist, and the Greek participle says the same: the authorities which actually are. Paul's claim is that civil authority as such is a divine institution and that the particular authorities in place hold their office by God's ordination, which in his own day meant a pagan empire. Two things are said about the magistrate's commission. He is “the minister of God to thee for good”, so his office is a service and has an end; and “he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil”, so the sword is genuinely his, and the power of the sword is not the church's. The dictionary reads this within the classical Reformed framework: family, church, and state are three God-ordained authorities, each with its proper sphere, and all three under the lordship of Christ. Subjection is therefore the Christian's ordinary duty, owed for conscience' sake and not merely for fear. It is not unlimited. When the authorities commanded the apostles not to preach, the answer given was that we ought to obey God rather than men — a refusal to obey a particular command, offered without rebellion against the office itself and with the penalty accepted.

corruption_summary: The text is used either to sanctify whatever a government does, or dismissed so that Christ's lordship is confined to the private sphere; both lose the magistrate's accountable commission.
corruption_paragraphs: The first abuse makes Romans 13 a blank endorsement. Because the powers that be are ordained of God, every command is treated as binding and every protest as rebellion, a reading used historically to silence resistance to real tyranny. The passage itself supplies the limit. Authority is given for a stated end — the minister of God to thee for good, a revenger upon him that doeth evil — and a commission with a purpose can be exceeded. The apostles who wrote and received this letter also answered a magistrate's order with the words that we ought to obey God rather than men, and took the flogging that followed. Obedience to God where the two conflict is not a denial of the ordinance but a recognition of who ordained it.

The second abuse is the modern Radical Two-Kingdoms position, which severs the civil sphere from the lordship of Christ altogether, so that the state is governed by its own autonomous standard and the church has nothing to say to it. The dictionary affirms the classical two-kingdoms doctrine of the Reformers, which distinguishes the spheres of church and magistrate and their proper instruments — the word for one, the sword for the other — without conceding that any sphere lies outside Christ's reign. Romans 13 says the magistrate is God's minister, which is a title of accountability before it is a title of dignity. The principle to recover is that the Christian owes real subjection for conscience' sake, that the sword belongs to the magistrate and not to the church, and that the magistrate himself will answer to the One whose minister he is.

pos: n. phr. (a title of God, in both Testaments)
etymology: Hebrew esh oklah — esh, fire, and akal, to eat or devour; rendered in Greek pyr katanaliskon. The figure is of a fire that eats what it touches rather than merely burning.
biblical_def: The phrase is a title of God and is identical in both Testaments. Moses says, “For the LORD thy God is a consuming fire, even a jealous God,” and the writer to the Hebrews, after describing the shaking of earth and heaven, concludes, “For our God is a consuming fire.” The continuity is the point worth pressing, since it is commonly supposed that the severity belongs to the older covenant. Hebrews quotes it of our God, in a letter written to Christians, as the ground of an exhortation to serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear. The Hebrew joins the title to jealousy, and the two interpret each other: a jealous God is not petty but exclusive in His covenant claim, and the fire is the energy of that claim against whatever rivals it. Deuteronomy also sets the figure on the side of Israel — “as a consuming fire he shall destroy them” — so the same attribute that is terrible to the enemy goes before the covenant people as their advance guard. Scripture nowhere offers this as one option among the divine attributes to be balanced against love; God is a consuming fire, and the believer approaches Him in Christ, who is the reason the fire does not consume those who come.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Consuming, destroying; wasting; devouring. A consuming fire, Deuteronomy 4:24 and Hebrews 12:29, a title of God, joined in Deuteronomy to His jealousy.
webster_full: Consuming, wasting, destroying, devouring, bringing to an end.

corruption_summary: The title is assigned to an Old Testament deity supposedly superseded by a gentler New Testament one, although Hebrews applies it to the God Christians now worship.
corruption_paragraphs: The oldest form of this error is Marcion's, which set a severe creator against the merciful Father of Jesus; the church condemned it in the second century, and it has returned in every age since. Its present form is popular rather than systematic: congregations are taught, by selection and by silence, that wrath and jealousy characterise the earlier Scriptures while the New Testament reveals a God of love alone. Hebrews 12:29 is decisive against it. The author takes Moses' sentence, applies it without softening to the God Christians worship, and makes it the reason for reverence and godly fear in New Covenant worship. The severity is not superseded; it is the ground of an argument addressed to the church.

The second corruption is the domestication of worship that follows. Where God is no longer understood as a consuming fire, reverence is an unintelligible category, and worship is designed for comfort and approachability. Hebrews 12 reasons the other way: precisely because we receive a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear. Nor does this set fire against love, which would be its own error; the fire is the energy of a jealous covenant love that will not share its people. The principle to recover is that the believer draws near with boldness through Christ and with awe at the same moment, and that a God who could not consume would not be worth the reverence.

pos: n. phr. (the reward Moses had respect unto, Hebrews 11:26)
etymology: Greek misthapodosia, a payment of wages, from misthos, wages or hire, and apodidōmi, to give back; with English recompence, from Latin recompensare, to repay.
biblical_def: The phrase belongs to the account of Moses in the roll of faith: “Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward.” The Greek misthapodosia is a wage-paying word, and the writer uses it deliberately, for he has already told his readers not to cast away their confidence, “which hath great recompence of reward”, and will shortly say that God “is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him”. The verse describes a calculation. Moses weighed two sets of riches — the treasures of Egypt, immediate and certain, against the reproach of Christ with a reward not yet seen — and esteemed, that is reckoned, the reproach to be the greater wealth. Faith here is not a leap against evidence but an accounting that takes God's promise as a real asset. This raises the question that must be answered carefully, since Scripture is emphatic that salvation is not of works lest any man should boast. The reward is not a wage earned; it is itself of grace, promised freely to those who believe, and the ground of a believer's acceptance is Christ's righteousness imputed and never his own performance. But the promise, once given, is a real thing to be reckoned with, and Hebrews presents Moses as a man who reckoned with it and acted accordingly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Recompence, an equivalent returned for any thing given, done, or suffered; reward. The recompence of the reward, Hebrews 11:26, that which Moses had respect unto, esteeming it greater riches than Egypt's treasures.

corruption_summary: Reward is either preached as wages earned, which overturns justification by faith, or denied altogether as unworthy, which contradicts the plain promises Scripture holds out as motive.
corruption_paragraphs: The first error turns the reward into a wage and the Christian life into a transaction. Roman Catholic teaching on merit, and the popular evangelical bargaining that treats obedience and giving as deposits against future returns, both make the same move: the believer earns, and God pays. Scripture forecloses it. Salvation is by grace through faith, not of works lest any man should boast, and the only righteousness in which a sinner stands is Christ's imputed to him. Hebrews 11 itself is a chapter about faith, and Moses is commended not for a work performed but for a valuation made.

The opposite error, and the likelier one in Reformed circles, is to be embarrassed by reward altogether, as though any regard for it were mercenary and the only pure motive were disinterested love. That is a higher standard than the Bible sets. Our Lord motivates by reward repeatedly in the Sermon on the Mount, Paul runs to obtain a crown, and Hebrews says plainly that the man who comes to God must believe that He is a rewarder. The reward is itself grace, which is what keeps it from being a wage; and the content of it is God Himself, which is what keeps it from being mercenary. The principle to recover is Moses' own method: to reckon the unseen promise as the greater riches, and then to choose by that reckoning rather than by what is immediately in hand.

pos: n. phr. (death, as the common road of mankind)
etymology: Hebrew derek kol ha-arets — derek, a way, road, or course, and erets, the earth or land. The idiom names death as the road everyone on earth travels.
biblical_def: The phrase occurs twice in the Authorized Version, and in both places it is a dying man's own description of what is happening to him. Joshua, old and full of days, gathers Israel and says, “behold, this day I am going the way of all the earth: and ye know in all your hearts and in all your souls, that not one thing hath failed of all the good things which the LORD your God spake concerning you.” David charges Solomon with the same words: “I go the way of all the earth: be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man.” The idiom names death as the common road, the course every man on earth takes, and its plainness is its strength: neither man reaches for a euphemism or asks for sympathy. What is striking is what each does with the announcement. Both treat their own dying as the proper occasion for a testimony and a charge. Joshua's first use of his last hours is to certify God's faithfulness — not one thing hath failed — putting the whole weight of his life behind the reliability of the promises. David's is to command courage and manhood in his son. Scripture gives no deathbed sentimentality here. The way of all the earth is stated as a fact, and the fact is made the platform for witness and for the handing on of duty.

corruption_summary: Death has been made unmentionable and professionally managed, so the plain speech of Joshua and David about their own dying sounds alien, and the deathbed loses its office of testimony.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. It faces a culture that has removed death from speech and from sight. Dying has moved from the house to the institution, the vocabulary has softened into passing and losing, and the frank announcement — I go the way of all the earth — strikes modern ears as harsh. The softening is not kindness. It leaves the dying isolated in a knowledge no one around them will name, and it deprives the living of the one certainty that orders every other plan. Moses prays to be taught to number his days, and a man who cannot say the word cannot number them.

The office these two passages model is worth recovering deliberately. Joshua and David both treat their last hours as a trust: one certifies that God kept every promise, the other charges his son to be strong and shew himself a man. Neither is performing resignation, and neither is pretending. They are doing the work that belongs to a believer's death — testifying to God's faithfulness while the testimony still costs something, and handing on duty to those who remain. It is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment, and Scripture treats that appointment as a reason for plain speech rather than for silence. The principle to recover is that a Christian's dying is his last and often his loudest sermon.

pos: n. phr. (the substance of the case, in Job's reply to his friends)
etymology: Hebrew shoresh dabar — shoresh, a root, and dabar, a word, thing, or matter. The figure takes the root as what is hidden beneath and gives the thing its life.
biblical_def: The phrase comes in Job's answer to Bildad, immediately after the great confession of the Redeemer: “For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth.” A few verses later Job turns on his friends: “But ye should say, Why persecute we him, seeing the root of the matter is found in me?” The Hebrew dabar means a word, a thing, or a case, and shoresh is a root; the idiom names the substance of a case, the thing hidden beneath that gives the whole its life, as a root does a tree. Job's claim is that if his friends looked beneath his circumstances they would find the real matter in him — a genuine fear of God, which the narrator and God Himself both attest — and that this should have stopped their persecution. The counsellors had been reasoning from the surface, arguing backwards from his losses to a hidden guilt. Job answers that the root is there to be found and that they have not looked for it. The English idiom to get to the root of the matter descends from this verse, and its ordinary use is not far from the sense: to reach the real substance beneath appearances rather than judging by what shows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Root, that part of a plant which enters the earth and draws nourishment; the original or cause of any thing. The root of the matter, Job 19:28, the substance or real ground of the case.
webster_full: Root, that part of a plant which enters the earth and imbibes nourishment.

corruption_summary: Job's friends judged a man by his visible circumstances and reasoned backward to hidden guilt — a method still common, and still condemned by the book's own ending.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error it exposes is perennial and lives comfortably inside the church. Job's counsellors held a tidy doctrine of retribution — suffering indicates sin — and applied it to a man whom God Himself had called perfect and upright. Its modern descendants are easy to recognise: the assumption that illness or poverty or long trouble implies a hidden fault, a want of faith, or a failure to claim something; and, in its prosperity form, the inversion that makes visible blessing the proof of God's approval. Both read the surface and pronounce on the root, and the book ends with God's anger kindled against the friends for not having spoken of Him the thing that is right.

Job's complaint is that they never looked for the root at all. They argued from his circumstances to his character, when the root of the matter was in him and findable — a real fear of God, attested in the first chapter before any of the suffering began. The principle to recover is twofold and pastoral. In judging others, the visible case is not the substance, and a comforter who reasons backward from affliction to guilt is doing what God rebuked. In examining oneself, the question is the same one: whether the root is there, whether beneath the circumstances the real thing is present, since the root is precisely what does not show and is exactly what matters.

pos: n. phr. (this present life, as the sphere where God's goodness is seen)
etymology: Hebrew erets chayyim — erets, land or earth, and chayyim, the living or life. The idiom names the realm of those still alive, as distinguished from the grave.
biblical_def: The phrase occurs some fifteen times in the Authorized Version and names this present life as a territory — the country of those still alive, over against the grave. Its three characteristic uses are easily traced. It is where God's goodness is looked for: “I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living.” It is where He is to be walked before and served: “I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living.” And its loss is the sting of dying, as Hezekiah says on receiving his sentence, “I shall not see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living: I shall behold man no more with the inhabitants of the world.” The gravest use is Isaiah's of the Suffering Servant: “he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.” That line gives the phrase its full weight in Christian reading. The believer hopes to see God's goodness in the land of the living because One was cut off out of it in his place. Taken together the uses assume what the modern mind doubts — that this life is a real and bounded sphere, that there is a door out of it, and that what is done here is done once.

corruption_summary: This life is treated either as all there is, or as a mere waiting room of no account; Scripture calls it a bounded land where God's goodness is really seen and where men really walk before Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The secular assumption is that the land of the living is the whole map. On that premise every hope must be cashed within the span, which explains the age's frantic relation to time — the pursuit of legacy, the refusal of ageing, the treatment of death as a medical failure rather than an appointment. Scripture agrees that this life matters intensely and denies that it is the whole. The psalmist expects to see the goodness of the LORD here, in the land of the living, and the expectation is what kept him from fainting; but he knows the land has a border, and Hezekiah's lament shows exactly where it runs.

The opposite error belongs to Christians and is the more surprising of the two. Here this life is discounted as a waiting room, its work and relationships and bodily goods treated as of no lasting account, with a piety that is really a disguised impatience. The phrase itself rebukes it. The land of the living is where God's goodness is to be seen and where His servants are to walk before Him, and the Psalms treat both as serious business. The deepest word remains Isaiah's, that the Servant was cut off out of the land of the living for the transgression of His people. The principle to recover is that this life is a real country with a real border, given for walking before God in; that the believer may expect to see God's goodness within it; and that his standing beyond the border was purchased by One who was cut off out of it.
